transcript:
Header: 2026-06-12 15:00 PDT — 75 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Arjun Gupta (Redwood SA), Sofia Martinez (Archimedes CTO), Ethan Park (Archimedes ML), Priya Rao (Archimedes Infra), Daniel Kim (Archimedes Security)

[00:00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining — quick intro round, we'll focus on prefix caching strategy for your production LLM workloads.
[00:00:18] Sofia: Yep thanks. high level we have a multi-tenant inference platform internally, want to reduce per-token cost and tail latency for our chat assistant.
[00:00:32] Liam: Great, can you outline current traffic profile? like prompt length, common prefixes, percent system prompts vs user prompts?
[00:00:46] Ethan: Sure — most prompts are 60–180 tokens, with about 40% identical system prefixes (policy + persona). We also have many templated prompts where first 50 tokens are near-identical. 70% of requests are low-variance conversational follow-ups.
[00:01:05] Priya: infra note — we're running GKE on private subnet with strict egress; for now on-prem eval could be interesting.
[00:01:20] Arjun: good to know. so prefix caching would target those repeated system prompts and template heads to cache KV cache snapshots to avoid re-computing early layers, correct?
[00:01:34] Ethan: Exactly. curious about hit-rate expectations and whether we can rely on cache to reduce GPU work by say 30–50%.

[00:05:00] Liam: high-level: hit-rate is function of how you form cache keys and the variability of the prefix. If you namespace per-tenant and canonicalize whitespace/tokenization, we often see 20–60% hit rates depending on workload. For templates with stable system prompts you get higher hit rates.
[00:05:22] Daniel: when you say namespace per-tenant, do you mean separate key prefixes or physically separate KV stores? security concern here is cache poisoning or cross-tenant leakage.
[00:05:40] Arjun: two approaches: logical namespace (key prefix + tenant id) or physical isolation (per-tenant KV instance). Logical is simpler and used in hosted mode; for strict compliance we'd recommend physical separation for Private/on-prem.
[00:05:58] Priya: physical separation has higher ops overhead — what about encryption and KMS?
[00:06:10] Liam: you can encrypt cached snapshots with tenant-specific KMS keys. On Private we support customer-managed KMS/HSM. That plus key prefixing provides multi-tenant safety without full physical separation.

[00:10:20] Ethan: how do you handle slightly different prefixes — e.g., templated prompts with user name inserted early? That would break exact matching.
[00:10:35] Liam: common pattern: token-level normalization and parameterization. Replace user-specific tokens with placeholders before hashing into cache key. Also consider longest-common-prefix hashing where we store multiple checkpoint points for common split positions.
[00:10:52] Maya: practical tradeoff is how many checkpoints you keep; more increases memory but raises hit-rate and reduces recompute.

[00:15:00] Sofia: eviction policy — LRU? TTL? predictive?
[00:15:12] Liam: typically LRU with soft TTL plus frequency weighting works well. We also add size-aware eviction because KV snapshots for long sequence lengths are larger. For multi-tenant clusters we apply per-tenant quotas to avoid noisy neighbor eviction.
[00:15:34] Ethan: curious about stale state: if model weights change (new model version) or quantization changes, cached checkpoints invalidated?
[00:15:48] Arjun: yes cache key must incorporate model_version, quantization profile, and runtime flags (e.g., attention optimization toggles). We include a cache versioning namespace so we never serve incompatible snapshots.

[00:20:00] Priya: on the topic of quantization: if we serve both int8 and fp16 variants, can we reuse checkpoints across quantization formats?
[00:20:12] Liam: not safely. Different quantization can change activation representation; we treat quantization as part of the cache key. However with certain mixed-precision flavors we can store a float32 checkpoint and transcode to int8 on load but that's expensive. So better to keep separate snapshots per quant profile.

[00:25:00] Ethan: batching interaction: if we serve batches of requests, how does prefix caching work with dynamic batching?
[00:25:16] Liam: prefix cache reduces token computation for the prefix portion; when batching occurs we can merge KV caches for identical prefixes in a batch. For heterogeneous prefixes we still get savings for items with hits. There's also an optimization where we maintain a shared prefix pool and during batching we detect identical checkpoint signatures and only run decoder steps for unique states.
[00:25:40] Maya: but that requires runtime support to stack different KV shapes. Our runtime supports variable-length KV and efficient merging, but on some older GPUs there're kernel constraints — that's why we probe device kernel capabilities in model profile stage.

[00:30:00] Daniel: security question — could a tenant infer another tenant's usage by probing cache latency or hit/miss patterns? Basically side-channel risk.
[00:30:18] Arjun: we mitigate via constant-time responses for cache metadata at the API layer, and per-tenant quotas so tenant A can't cause thrashing affecting B. Also we don't expose hit/miss counts to tenants by default; metrics are aggregated.
[00:30:36] Daniel: good. also wanting audit logs for evictions and key namespace activities.
[00:30:44] Liam: Redwood Console includes audit trails for cache operations in Dedicated/Private builds — we can add per-tenant audit hooks to ship to your SIEM.

[00:35:00] Ethan: let's talk about measuring effective hit-rate — is it server-side token savings or end-to-end latency impact?
[00:35:10] Liam: measure both. hit-rate is proportion of requests that hit a cached checkpoint at the decision point. Token-savings is estimated by prefix_length * hit_rate. But actual latency depends on batching, network RTTs (esp for VPC/on-prem) and cache lookup time. We recommend a small e2e benchmark: record baseline p50/p95 and repeat with cache enabled and the same traffic.

[00:40:00] Sofia: for our on-prem constraint, egress is limited — what's the easiest deployment? Private with customer-managed control plane?
[00:40:12] Maya: yes Private deployment in your VPC or on-prem package; we support a local KV cache with Redis or RocksDB backed store. For strict air-gapped we can provide appliance image.
[00:40:30] Priya: does Redwood require a central control plane out-of-band?
[00:40:36] Arjun: optional. you can run fully private with no Redwood-hosted control plane; in that case we ship the full admin bundle and KMS integration.

[00:45:00] Ethan: any gotchas with GPU memory when storing many checkpoints?
[00:45:12] Liam: KV checkpoints are stored off-GPU in KV store and streamed to GPU as needed. But the runtime caches hot checkpoints in GPU memory to avoid transfer overhead. So you must size GPU memory or set hot-cache size limits. We provide tooling to estimate memory usage given checkpoint count and average token length.

[00:50:00] Sofia: benchmark ask — we want to see p95 improvements for our top-50 templates and cost delta.
[00:50:12] Maya: agreed — next step we'll run a targeted benchmark using your top-200 prefixes. If you share sample traffic Ethan, we can replay it in our test harness.

[00:55:00] Daniel: one more security — KMS key rotation — how do you invalidate caches when keys rotate?
[00:55:12] Arjun: cache entries encrypted with KMS include key version metadata. On rotate, we re-encrypt new snapshots as they're written; old snapshots can be invalidated by bumping cache namespace or via a key-version check at load time. We'll document recommended rotation cadence and invalidation procedure.

[01:05:00] Ethan: curious about operational metrics — what should we track?
[01:05:10] Liam: hit-rate per-tenant, token-savings, p50/p95 latency delta, cache size per tenant, eviction rate, cache-entry age distribution, and cache-miss origin (client-side variance vs TTL). Also track model-version mismatches.

[01:10:00] Maya: recap and next steps: we'll share design doc/configs, run benchmarks, and provide security docs. Schedule follow-up demo for Private KV deployment.
[01:10:18] Sofia: sounds good — thanks everyone.
[01:11:00] Maya: I'll email notes and next steps. thanks all for time.

End of transcript.
